40187: Many of Jesus' miracles echo Elisha: he feeds a crowd with a few loaves and has leftovers (compare 2 Kgs 4:42-44 with Mark 6:35-44), raises the dead, and heals a leper. In Nazareth Jesus points to Naaman, a foreign enemy healed by Israel's God, as a sign of God's grace to outsiders (Luke 4:27). Elijah's ascension and the passing of his spirit to Elisha are echoed in Jesus' ascension and the giving of the Spirit to his disciples (Acts 1:8-11; Acts 2:1-4). The last scene of 2 Kings, David's heir lifted from prison to the king's table, has been read by Christian interpreters as a seed of hope fulfilled in the Son of David who is raised and enthroned. Jewish readers likewise see in Jehoiachin's release the survival of David's line; his grandson Zerubbabel led the return (1 Chr 3:17-19; Ezra 3:2).
40188: Elisha and the 'little children' mauled by bears
40189: Sceptics cite 2 Kgs 2:23-24 as proof of a petty, cruel God who killed small children for teasing a bald man; some popular preaching uses it simply to warn children not to mock adults.
40190: The Hebrew *ne'arim qetannim* can mean 'young men' or 'youths'; *na'ar* is used for adults such as Joseph at 17 and soldiers. The scene is at Bethel, the centre of Jeroboam's calf worship, and a large group (at least 42) confronts the new prophet with 'go up, thou bald head', possibly mocking Elijah's ascension and telling Elisha to disappear too. The episode reads as a rejection of God's prophet by an apostate city, echoing the covenant curse of wild animals (Lev 26:21-22).
40191: Evangelical commentators such as Iain Provan and Dale Ralph Davis argue for this contextual reading. Some scholars still find the story troubling and admit the text gives few details. Critics like Burke Long see it as a legend from a prophetic guild exalting Elisha's authority. Most agree it is not about children teasing a bald man.
40192: Reading the scene in its covenant setting shows that rejecting God's word had real consequences in Israel's life, without turning the story into a fairy tale about grumpy prophets.
40193: Good kings are rewarded, bad kings punished, at once
40194: Kings teaches a simple formula: obey God and you will prosper; disobey and you will be punished, in your own lifetime.
40195: Kings is more complex. Manasseh, the worst king, reigns 55 years (2 Kgs 21:1); Josiah, the best, dies young in battle (2 Kgs 23:29). Judgment comes on the nation over generations, after long patience, and good reforms can delay but not cancel it (2 Kgs 22:18-20; 2 Kgs 23:26). The book's theology is covenantal and corporate. Scholars note that Chronicles, by contrast, shows more immediate consequences, and the two books together give a fuller picture.
40196: Evangelical scholars agree that Kings shows God's long patience and delayed judgment, while affirming that it does teach real cause and effect between covenant faithfulness and national fate. The popular formula is generally acknowledged as an oversimplification.
40197: Kings helps readers understand why the righteous suffer and the wicked sometimes flourish, and that God's justice works across history, not always on our timetable.
40198: 2 Kings helped exiles grieve honestly, admit their sin, recognise that God's word through the prophets had come true, and hold on to the thin thread of hope in David's surviving heir.
40199: 2 Kings speaks to nations and churches about the long-term consequences of unfaithfulness, the courage of reformers, the danger of relying on political alliances, God's care for outsiders like Naaman, and hope that survives catastrophe.
40200: 1 Chronicles retells Israel's story from Adam to David for a small community back from exile, to show that they still belong to God's people and that worship at the temple is the heart of their identity.
40201: The Chronicler (anonymous); Ezra by Jewish tradition
40202: An unnamed writer, usually called 'the Chronicler', probably a Levite or someone close to the Levitical singers and gatekeepers of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. The Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a) names Ezra.
40203: The writer's deep interest in Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple service, often adding material not found in Samuel-Kings (1 Chr 15:16-24; 1 Chr 23-26), points to temple circles. The genealogy of David's descendants runs several generations after the exile (1 Chr 3:17-24), so the work dates from at least the late 5th or 4th century BC. The ending of 2 Chronicles overlaps with the start of Ezra (2 Chr 36:22-23; Ezra 1:1-3), which long suggested the same author; since the 1960s-70s Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson have argued from differences in language and theology that they are separate works.
40204: 2 Chronicles (one book with 1 Chronicles in the Hebrew Bible)
40205: Ezra-Nehemiah (traditional and older critical view, now widely questioned)
40206: Jerusalem in the Persian province of Yehud
40207: Probably written in Jerusalem around the Second Temple, sometime between about 400 and 300 BC. Some date it earlier (c. 520-500 BC, near the temple's rebuilding) and a few later, in the early Hellenistic period.
40209: Jerusalem and the small province of Yehud
40210: The returned community was tiny, poor, ruled by Persia, with no king and a modest temple. Were they still God's people? Did the promises to David still matter? Chronicles answers by linking them, through genealogies, to Adam, Abraham and the twelve tribes, and by showing David organising the worship they still practised.
40211: The genealogies (1 Chr 1-9) run from Adam to the post-exilic community. The narrative (1 Chr 10-29) covers Saul's death and David's reign, c. 1010-970 BC, ending with Solomon's accession.
40212: Cyrus of Persia conquers Babylon and allows exiles to return; the Cyrus Cylinder describes his policy of restoring peoples and temples.
40213: The Second Temple is completed in Jerusalem.
40215: Jews at Elephantine in Egypt write to Persian officials asking to rebuild their temple, showing Jewish communities spread across the empire.
40216: Alexander the Great conquers the Persian Empire, including Judah.
40217:
Chronicles was written a century or more after the return from exile. Judah (Yehud) was a small Persian province about 40 kilometres across, with a population of perhaps 20,000-30,000. There was no king; the high priest and Persian governor held authority. The rebuilt temple was smaller than Solomon's, and some older people had wept when they saw its foundations (Ezra 3:12). The community's questions were about identity and continuity: are we the same Israel that God chose? Is God still with us?

The Chronicler answers by rewriting history. Using Samuel and Kings as a main source (often word for word), he selects, omits and adds. He starts with nine chapters of genealogy from Adam, placing the community within the whole human story and within all twelve tribes, not just Judah. He then tells the story of David, but leaves out David's struggle with Saul, his adultery with Bathsheba and Absalom's revolt. Instead he focuses on David bringing the ark to Jerusalem, organising the Levites and singers, receiving God's covenant and preparing everything for the temple Solomon will build. Almost a third of the David story is about worship.

Some readers have called this whitewashing. Scholars today generally see it differently: the Chronicler's readers already knew Samuel-Kings, and he was not trying to replace them but to draw out lessons for a new situation, much as the four Gospels each tell Jesus' story with different emphases. Sara Japhet, H. G. M. Williamson and others have shown his careful theological purpose. He does include David's sinful census (1 Chr 21), because it leads to the purchase of the temple site.

The Greek translators called the book *Paraleipomena*, 'things left out', thinking it was a supplement to Kings. The Hebrew title *Divrei ha-Yamim* means 'the events of the days'. Jerome suggested it be called a 'chronicle of the whole of sacred history', which gave us the English title.
40219: In a collectivist culture, who you descend from defines who you are and what you may do: inherit land, serve as priest, belong to the assembly. The genealogies say: you are still Israel.
40220: The Chronicler keeps saying 'all Israel': the twelve tribes together, not only Judah. He hopes for a reunited people around the temple.
40222: Levites assisted priests, guarded gates and led music. David organises them into divisions; the Chronicler gives music a prophetic role.
40224: Uzzah's death happened because the ark was put on a cart; David now has Levites carry it on poles 'according to the word of the LORD'.
40226: David cannot build the temple because he shed much blood; Solomon, a 'man of rest' whose name echoes shalom (peace), will build it.
40228: The Chronicler cites prophetic records (Samuel, Nathan, Gad) and royal annals. Ancient historians shaped their sources openly for teaching purposes.
40229:
In most printed Hebrew Bibles, following the order in the Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b), Chronicles is the last book of the Tanakh. The whole Hebrew Bible therefore runs from Adam (Gen 1; 1 Chr 1:1) to Cyrus' call to 'go up' to Jerusalem (2 Chr 36:23), a story of creation, exile and return. A rabbinic saying holds that Chronicles was given only to be interpreted (*lidrosh*, Leviticus Rabbah 1:3), meaning its lists and names hide teaching. The Talmud (Megillah 13a), for example, reads the obscure 'Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh' (1 Chr 4:18) as the princess who rescued Moses, rewarded by being called 'daughter of the LORD' (Bithiah).

Chronicles shaped Jewish prayer. David's psalm when the ark arrives (1 Chr 16:8-36) and David's blessing at the end of his life (1 Chr 29:10-13: 'Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory...') are recited in the daily morning service. The latter's words also influenced the ending added to the Lord's Prayer in many manuscripts. The book's emphasis on music, singers and praise has made it a resource for liturgy in synagogue and church.

The first audience would hear 1 Chronicles as a message of belonging. Their names were written into Israel's family tree, from Adam onwards. The David they met was the founder of their worship, the king who said 'all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee' (1 Chr 29:14) and 'we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers' (1 Chr 29:15). A small, powerless community could still give generously, worship joyfully and trust that God's covenant with David was not finished.
40231: Nine chapters trace humanity, Abraham's line, the twelve tribes and the returned community, focusing on Judah, Levi and Benjamin.
40233: Saul died for unfaithfulness and for not seeking the LORD, so the kingdom passed to David.
40235: The tribes come together to anoint David, take Jerusalem and gather his mighty men.
40236: After the failure with Uzzah, the ark is carried properly with Levites and music; David appoints worship leaders.
40237: God promises David a lasting house and that his son will build the temple.
40239: David's census brings plague, but leads to the purchase of the threshing floor where the temple will stand.
40241: David gathers materials, organises priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers, and hands Solomon the plans.
40243: The people give freely; David blesses God and Solomon becomes king.
40269: To seek, enquire of or devote oneself to God. The Chronicler's key verb for true faith.
40271: Breach of trust, treachery toward God, especially in worship. It explains Saul's fall and the exile.
40272: Peace from enemies. Solomon is a 'man of rest', and the temple is a 'house of rest' for the ark.
40274: 'Give thanks': the opening of David's psalm and a refrain of Levitical worship, 'for his mercy endureth for ever'.
40276: To give freely and gladly. The people's generous giving for the temple is a model of joyful worship.
40277: Chronicles uses Samuel as a source, often word for word, but omits David's sins and family turmoil except the census.
40278: The genealogies begin with Adam and follow Genesis' lines of descent.
40279: David's thanksgiving psalm in 1 Chr 16 combines parts of Ps 105, Ps 96 and Ps 106.
40280: Chronicles and Ezra share the post-exilic setting, the focus on temple and Levites, and the overlapping verses about Cyrus.
40281: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, like Chronicles, uses a structured family tree to present identity and the Davidic hope.
40282: Chronicles keeps the Davidic hope alive when no Davidic king reigns: it traces David's line well past the exile (1 Chr 3:17-24) and records God's promise to establish his son's throne forever (1 Chr 17:11-14). In the Chronicler's version, God says 'I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever' (1 Chr 17:14), tying the king to God's own kingdom, which Christians read as pointing to Jesus as the Son of David who reigns in God's kingdom. Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy shaped like Chronicles' (Matt 1:1-17), and the theme of a new temple built by David's son is applied to Jesus and the church (John 2:19-21; Eph 2:19-22). Jewish readers see in Chronicles the continuing promise of a Davidic Messiah and the centrality of temple worship, now expressed in prayer until the temple is restored.
40283: The Prayer of Jabez as a formula for blessing
40284: Bruce Wilkinson's bestselling *The Prayer of Jabez* (2000) encouraged believers to pray Jabez's words daily (1 Chr 4:10), asking God to 'enlarge my coast', expecting God to expand their influence and blessings.
40285: Jabez's prayer is a two-verse note inside a long genealogy of Judah. His name sounds like the Hebrew for 'pain', and his prayer asks God to reverse that omen: to bless him, enlarge his territory (literal land), be with him and keep him from harm. In the Chronicler's theology it illustrates a key theme: those who call on God are heard. Scholars note it is an example of seeking God, not a formula.
40286: Supporters argue the text does commend Jabez ('more honourable than his brethren') and that God 'granted him that which he requested', so asking boldly for blessing is biblical. Evangelical critics, including many Reformed writers, worried that the book encouraged a mechanical, self-focused prayer. Both sides agree that God hears prayer; the question is whether this verse is a pattern to repeat or an example of trust.
40287: Reading Jabez in context keeps prayer relational, an act of trust in a covenant God, rather than a technique for success.
40288: Chronicles as an unreliable, sanitised history
40289: Some readers (and some older critics) see Chronicles as a whitewash that hides David's sins and is therefore less trustworthy than Samuel-Kings; others try to harmonise every difference.
40290: The Chronicler assumes readers know Samuel-Kings and writes a theological retelling for a new audience, like a sermon on familiar history. He includes sins when they serve his point (the census, 1 Chr 21). Scholars such as Sara Japhet, H. G. M. Williamson and Ralph Klein read his changes as deliberate interpretation; he also sometimes preserves older text forms (Samuel fragments from Qumran sometimes agree with Chronicles).
40291: Conservative scholars such as Raymond Dillard and Martin Selman accept that the Chronicler shapes his material theologically but hold that he used reliable sources and did not invent history. They harmonise some differences (e.g. the numbers) as scribal errors. Critics see more free composition. Both agree his purpose is teaching, not deception.
40292: Seeing Chronicles as a deliberate retelling helps readers appreciate how Scripture itself interprets earlier Scripture for new situations.
40293: 1 Chronicles told a small, discouraged community that they belonged to the great family of Israel stretching back to Adam, that worship at the temple was their life's centre, and that God's promise to David still stood.
40294: 1 Chronicles speaks to communities that feel small and marginal: you belong to a long story; worship and generosity matter; God's promises are not cancelled by weakness. It also shows how to retell history to draw out lessons for new generations.
40295: 2 Chronicles retells the story of Solomon and the kings of Judah to show that when God's people seek him and humble themselves he heals and restores, and it ends with an open door home.
40296: The same writer as 1 Chronicles, probably a Levite connected with the Second Temple in Persian-period Jerusalem.
40297: The style, theology and interests (temple, Levites, 'seeking' God, all Israel) are continuous with 1 Chronicles. The writer reworks 1-2 Kings, cites other sources such as 'the book of Nathan the prophet' and 'the visions of Iddo the seer' (2 Chr 9:29) and 'the story [midrash] of the prophet Iddo' (2 Chr 13:22), and adds material on Judah's kings not found in Kings. Scholars debate how much of this comes from lost sources and how much is the Chronicler's own composition.
40298: Most scholars place the writing in Jerusalem in the 4th century BC, with the Second Temple in operation.
40300: The community lived under Persia, without a king and with a modest temple. They needed to know whether their worship mattered, whether their own generation could know God's blessing, and whether repentance was really possible after so great a judgment.
40301: From Solomon's accession (c. 971/970 BC) through the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC) to Cyrus' decree (538 BC). The book barely mentions the northern kingdom except where it touches Judah.
40302: Shishak (Shoshenq I) invades Judah; Chronicles gives a fuller account with a prophetic message (2 Chr 12:1-12).
40304: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple.
40305: Cyrus allows the exiles to return and rebuild the temple.
40306: Approximate time of writing, under Persian rule, when the Jerusalem temple is the centre of Jewish life.
40307:
2 Chronicles begins with Solomon's wisdom and devotes six chapters to building and dedicating the temple (2 Chr 2-7). In the Chronicler's version, fire falls from heaven on the sacrifices and God's glory fills the house so that the priests cannot enter (2 Chr 7:1-3). God's answer to Solomon's prayer includes the famous promise: 'If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land' (2 Chr 7:14). This verse is the key to the rest of the book.

After Solomon, the Chronicler follows only Judah. The north, which broke away from David's house and the temple, is mostly left out, though its people are always invited back (2 Chr 13:4-12; 2 Chr 30:1-12). Each king is a test case of the 2 Chr 7:14 principle. When Rehoboam is attacked by Shishak, he and his princes humble themselves, and the disaster is limited (2 Chr 12:6-7). Asa seeks God and has peace, but late in life relies on Aram and on physicians rather than God (2 Chr 16:7-12). Jehoshaphat prays 'we know not what to do: but our eyes are upon thee' and the enemy armies destroy each other while the Levites sing (2 Chr 20:12; 2 Chr 20:21-23).

This pattern has been called 'immediate retribution': blessing follows faithfulness and trouble follows sin within the same generation. Older critics like Julius Wellhausen saw it as artificial. More recent scholars (Japhet, Williamson, Raymond Dillard) argue it is a deliberate message for the post-exilic community: each generation stands before God for itself (compare Ezek 18), and no generation is trapped by its parents' sins. The most striking case is Manasseh, the worst king in Kings, who in Chronicles repents in Babylonian captivity and is restored (2 Chr 33:10-17), a living picture of exile and return.

The book ends with the exile explained as the land enjoying its sabbaths for seventy years, as Jeremiah prophesied (2 Chr 36:21; compare Lev 26:34-35; Jer 25:11), and then with Cyrus' decree. The final word in the Hebrew is *ve-ya'al*, 'and let him go up'.
40309: For the Chronicler, to 'seek' God is to turn to him in worship, prayer and trust, especially in crisis. Kings who seek him prosper; those who rely on foreign alliances fail.
40311: Singers lead the army, praising 'the beauty of holiness'. Worship is presented as a form of trust that God himself will fight.
40312: Prophets as messengers of second chances
40313: The Chronicler adds many prophets who warn kings, giving each a chance to repent before judgment.
40315: Hezekiah invites the remnant of the northern tribes to Jerusalem for Passover; when some come unclean, he prays and God pardons them, showing heart over ritual.
40317: Leviticus said the land would rest during exile to make up for neglected sabbath years. The Chronicler links this with Jeremiah's seventy years.
40319: King Uzziah enters the temple to burn incense, a priestly role, and is struck with skin disease: even kings must respect God's holiness.
40320:
In the Jewish canon 2 Chronicles is the last book of the Hebrew Bible. Its final verse is Cyrus' proclamation: 'Who is there among you of all his people? The LORD his God be with him, and let him go up' (2 Chr 36:23). The Hebrew Bible thus ends not with judgment but with an invitation to return to Jerusalem and rebuild God's house. The word for 'go up' (*'alah*) gives the modern Hebrew term *aliyah*, used both for immigrating to the land of Israel and for being called up to read the Torah in synagogue. Generations of Jews have felt this final verse as a call to hope and return.

The Chronicler's story of Manasseh's repentance (2 Chr 33:12-13) became a key text for rabbinic teaching on the power of repentance (*teshuvah*). Later Jewish writers composed a 'Prayer of Manasseh' imagining his words in captivity (it survives in Greek and is included in some Christian Bibles). The rabbis taught that the gates of repentance are never shut, and Manasseh became the classic proof. Hezekiah's prayer for the unclean worshippers (2 Chr 30:18-20) is also cited as showing that God looks on the heart that 'prepareth his heart to seek God'.

The first audience would have heard 2 Chronicles as a sermon on how to live as God's people now. The temple was rebuilt; the covenant was still open. Each generation could seek God, humble itself, pray and be heard. God is the one whose 'eyes run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him' (2 Chr 16:9). The relationship is not a cold ledger but a living covenant in which God is eager to forgive.
40322: Solomon asks for wisdom, builds the temple with Hiram's help and brings in the ark.
40324: Fire falls, glory fills the temple, and God promises to hear when his people humble themselves and pray.
40326: The north breaks away; Rehoboam, Abijah and Asa experience the results of forsaking or seeking the LORD.
40328: Facing invasion, Judah fasts and prays; singers lead the army and God gives victory.
40330: Joash, Amaziah and Uzziah start well and end badly through pride and apostasy.
40332: Hezekiah cleanses the temple and holds a Passover for all Israel; Josiah renews the covenant and keeps a great Passover.
40334: Taken to Babylon in chains, the worst king humbles himself and God restores him.
40336: Ignoring God's messengers, Judah falls; the land keeps its sabbaths until Cyrus invites the people home.
